questions.stimulusText:
Mara had volunteered to restore the brass bell from the town’s abandoned ferry landing. She imagined polishing away a little tarnish and finishing before lunch. Instead, she found a cracked wooden handle, layers of green corrosion, and a clapper frozen in place.
At the workshop, Mr. Ibarra showed her how to loosen each part without damaging it. Mara wanted to hurry, but every shortcut left a scratch or bent an edge. She began keeping notes: which solution worked, how long each piece soaked, and where every washer belonged.
On the morning of the river festival, Mara fastened the repaired bell beside the new walking path. The mayor invited her to ring it. She pulled the handle, but only a dull knock sounded. Her face warmed as the crowd waited. Then Mara noticed that the clapper’s leather strap had twisted during installation. She calmly removed the pin, straightened the strap, and tried again.
The clear note traveled over the water. Mara smiled, not because the bell sounded perfect, but because she now knew what to do when it did not.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why are deep-rooted plants useful in rain gardens?

choices.A: Their roots form channels that help water enter the soil.
choices.B: Their leaves prevent all rain from reaching the ground.
choices.C: Their flowers remove litter from nearby streams.
choices.D: Their stems strengthen building foundations.

questions.correctAnswer: Their roots form channels that help water enter the soil.
questions.explanation: The passage directly states that deep roots create channels in the soil.
questions.stimulusText:
After a heavy storm, water rushing from roofs and pavement can overwhelm drains and carry soil or litter into streams. A rain garden offers a small-scale solution. It is a shallow planted area placed where runoff naturally collects. Rather than sending water immediately into a pipe, the garden briefly holds it.
A rain garden is not a permanent pond. Its soil is prepared to absorb water, and its surface usually dries within a day or two. Deep-rooted native plants are often suitable because their roots create channels in the soil. These plants may also require less watering after they become established.
Location matters. Builders avoid placing rain gardens directly against foundations or over underground utilities. They also test how quickly the soil drains. If water remains too long, mosquitoes may breed and plant roots may decay.
One garden cannot prevent every flood. However, many small gardens distributed through a neighborhood can reduce the amount of runoff reaching storm drains at the same moment. They can also provide food and shelter for insects and birds. Thus, a feature designed to manage water may improve local habitat as well.

questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Summary
questions.prompt: Which sentence best summarizes the passage?

choices.A: Architectural features can provide evidence, but observers must interpret them thoughtfully.
choices.B: Old buildings should always be restored with local materials.
choices.C: Modern buildings contain fewer meaningful details than older ones.
choices.D: Decorative features are the most reliable clues to a building’s purpose.

questions.correctAnswer: Architectural features can provide evidence, but observers must interpret them thoughtfully.
questions.explanation: The passage presents buildings as records while warning readers against quick assumptions.
questions.stimulusText:
People often treat buildings as backgrounds, noticing them only when searching for an entrance. Yet a building can be read as evidence of the choices and needs of the people who made it. A wide staircase may announce a public gathering place. A row of identical windows may reveal that builders valued efficiency, while carved stone above a doorway may show where they chose to spend extra labor.
Materials provide clues, too. Brick made from nearby clay can connect a structure to its region. A later wall built with different brick may mark an expansion. Even repairs tell a story: a patch can show both where damage occurred and what materials were available when it was fixed.
Interpreting these clues requires caution. A modern visitor might assume that a tiny window was intended for decoration, although it may have reduced heat loss. One feature can also serve several purposes. An awning can shelter a doorway, shade a room, and advertise a shop.
Looking closely does not mean every guess will be correct. It means replacing a quick impression with useful questions: What problem did this feature solve? Which parts are original? What changed over time? Buildings become more than scenery when observers recognize them as records shaped by climate, technology, money, and human intention.

choices.C: The complete outline of one bird
choices.D: A row of squares beside the doorway

questions.correctAnswer: Three chalk marks beneath the roof edge
questions.explanation: The passage states that three chalk marks survived in the dry area beneath the roof edge.
questions.stimulusText:
Amaya and Tariq had spent two afternoons drawing a chalk grid across the brick wall behind the community center. The grid would guide a mural of birds crossing a sunrise, and each square corresponded to one square on their smaller sketch. By Friday evening, every line was in place.
A light rain arrived overnight. The wall beneath the roof edge stayed dry, but most of the grid faded into pale smudges. Tariq suggested beginning the mural anyway and judging the proportions by eye. Amaya looked at the wide blank wall, then at the detailed sketch. A small error in one corner, she realized, could grow into a crooked wing several feet away.
Three chalk marks had survived beneath the roof edge. Amaya measured the distance between them and compared it with the sketch. She and Tariq tied a string to the first mark, checked it with a level, and snapped fresh horizontal lines across the wall. Then they measured downward to rebuild the vertical lines.
The work delayed painting by an hour, but the new grid matched the original plan. At the unveiling, visitors noticed the bright birds, not the lines hidden beneath them. Amaya did. To her, the invisible grid was evidence that careful preparation could be rebuilt, even after it seemed to disappear.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What covers each gecko toe according to the passage?

choices.A: Millions of microscopic hairs
choices.B: A thin layer of natural glue
choices.C: Several flexible suction cups
choices.D: Rows of curved claws

questions.correctAnswer: Millions of microscopic hairs
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies millions of microscopic hairs as the structures covering each toe.
questions.stimulusText:
A gecko can race across a wall and pause on a ceiling without using glue, claws, or suction cups. The secret lies in structures too small to see without magnification. Each toe is covered with millions of microscopic hairs. Every hair branches into even finer tips that can make extremely close contact with a surface.
When those tips approach a wall, weak attractions form between molecules in the toe and molecules in the wall. One attraction is tiny, but millions acting together can support the gecko's weight. Because the hairs are flexible, they conform to small bumps and dips that would prevent a stiff surface from touching evenly.
Attachment alone would not be useful if the foot could not release. A gecko changes the angle of its toes as it steps. This motion peels the hair tips away in sequence, reducing their contact with the surface. The foot can therefore grip strongly in one position and release quickly in another.
Researchers study gecko feet while developing dry adhesives for robots and reusable fasteners. A successful material must do more than stick. It must also release on command, work repeatedly, and avoid leaving residue. The gecko's foot demonstrates how many weak contacts, arranged and controlled carefully, can produce a strong but reversible grip.

When those tips approach a wall, weak attractions form between molecules in the toe and molecules in the wall. One attraction is tiny, but millions acting together can support the gecko's weight. Because the hairs are flexible, they conform to small bumps and dips that would prevent a stiff surface from touching evenly.
Attachment alone would not be useful if the foot could not release. A gecko changes the angle of its toes as it steps. This motion peels the hair tips away in sequence, reducing their contact with the surface. The foot can therefore grip strongly in one position and release quickly in another.
Researchers study gecko feet while developing dry adhesives for robots and reusable fasteners. A successful material must do more than stick. It must also release on command, work repeatedly, and avoid leaving residue. The gecko's foot demonstrates how many weak contacts, arranged and controlled carefully, can produce a strong but reversible grip.

questions.stimulusText:
A screw may look simple, but its spiral ridge has several important measurements. The diameter, the distance between ridges, and the shape of each ridge determine which nut will fit. In early workshops, craftspeople often cut threads with tools made for their own shop. A bolt produced in one place might not match a nut made elsewhere, even when both appeared to be the same size.
As machines became more widely used, this mismatch created practical problems. A damaged bolt could delay a repair while a replacement was filed or recut by hand. Merchants also had to store many nearly identical parts because customers used different thread patterns.
Manufacturers gradually adopted shared sets of thread sizes. Gauges allowed workers to check whether a new bolt matched an agreed diameter and spacing. Printed tables helped workshops select the same measurements, and suppliers could label parts more consistently.
The change required effort. Some shops replaced cutting tools, updated records, and trained workers to use the new gauges. Standardization did not make every screw identical; different jobs still required different sizes and strengths. It created recognized families of parts. Once those families were widely understood, repairs became more predictable, inventories became simpler, and parts made in distant workshops were more likely to fit together.

choices.A: The lantern's latch is bent.
choices.B: The lantern has run out of fuel.
choices.C: She wants to buy padded pliers.
choices.D: She needs directions to the garden.

questions.correctAnswer: The lantern's latch is bent.
questions.explanation: Mina seeks repair because the bent latch prevents the glass door from closing.
questions.stimulusText:
Mina had promised to bring a lantern to the neighborhood’s evening garden walk. Her grandfather’s brass lantern seemed perfect until she discovered that its glass door would not close. With an hour remaining, she carried it to Mr. Bell’s repair shop.
Mr. Bell examined the bent latch. “I can straighten this,” he said, “but brass remembers every impatient hand.” Instead of reaching for a heavy tool, he warmed the latch beneath a small lamp and pressed it gradually with padded pliers. Mina watched the metal move by fractions.
“Wouldn’t hitting it be faster?” she asked.
“For a moment,” he replied. “Then we might spend tomorrow repairing what speed broke today.”
When the latch finally clicked, Mina polished the cloudy glass. At the walk, she carried the lantern at the rear of the group. Its modest circle of light did not illuminate the entire path, but it revealed each stone before someone stepped on it. Mina stopped wishing she had brought the brightest lantern. She began matching her pace to the people ahead, keeping the light where it was needed.
The next morning, she returned the lantern to its shelf. Beside it, she placed a note: “Handle slowly. Useful things do not have to hurry.”

questions.stimulusText:
The trail map showed one straight path to the overlook, and Eli had memorized every turn. Halfway up the hill, however, a fallen oak blocked the narrow trail. Its branches stretched into thorny brush on both sides.
Eli’s cousin Nia pointed to a faint path descending toward the creek. “The maintenance crew may use that route,” she said. Eli disliked walking downhill when their destination was above them, but climbing over the unstable trunk was clearly unsafe.
They followed the faint path. Near the creek, the trail disappeared beneath smooth stones. Nia noticed three small blue marks painted on rocks at regular intervals. The marks led upstream, crossed a wooden footbridge, and joined the main trail beyond the fallen tree.
At the overlook, Eli unfolded his map. The maintenance route was absent. He sketched it lightly in the margin, including the bridge and blue markers, but added a question mark beside the entrance. On the return trip, they met a ranger, who confirmed that the route was open temporarily while crews cleared the oak.
Eli erased the question mark and wrote “temporary detour.” He had always treated maps as finished answers. Now he understood them as records that sometimes needed careful updates from the ground beneath his feet.

questions.stimulusTitle: Why Some Cities Build Rain Gardens
questions.stimulusText:
During a storm, rain falling on roofs, sidewalks, and parking lots cannot soak directly into soil. Instead, it flows across these hard surfaces, gathering leaves, dirt, and other materials before entering street drains. A large volume arriving quickly can burden drainage systems and carry pollutants into streams.
A rain garden is a shallow planted basin designed to receive some of this runoff. Water enters the basin, spreads among grasses and flowering plants, and slowly filters through layers of soil. The garden is not a permanent pond. Designers select its depth, soil mixture, and drainage area so that standing water usually disappears within a day or two.
Plant choice matters. Deep-rooted native species can loosen soil and tolerate alternating wet and dry periods. Their stems also slow moving water. Yet a rain garden must be placed carefully. It should not sit over underground utilities or directly against a building foundation, and its size must match the area draining into it.
Rain gardens cannot prevent every flood or remove every pollutant. Their value comes from handling many smaller flows before those flows combine. When numerous properties use them, the gardens function like a scattered network of small sponges, reducing pressure on a city's drainage system while creating habitat for insects and birds.

questions.stimulusText:
When the community kitchen closed after Saturday’s bread workshop, Nia noticed a blue apron hanging behind the pantry door. Its pocket held a card covered with careful notes about oven temperatures. She assumed the apron belonged to Mr. Han, the instructor, but he had already left.
Nia could have placed it in the lost-and-found bin. Instead, she studied the card. One note mentioned that the old oven’s back corner heated fastest. Another warned that its timer rang two minutes late. The information would matter during Sunday’s charity bake sale, when volunteers unfamiliar with the kitchen would prepare dozens of loaves.
Nia called Mr. Han. The apron was not his; it belonged to Mrs. Ortiz, who had tested the oven all week. Mrs. Ortiz asked Nia to leave both items with the morning coordinator. Before going home, Nia copied the two most important warnings onto a large sheet and taped it beside the oven controls.
The next morning, volunteers rotated their pans and used a separate timer. By noon, every loaf had baked evenly. Mrs. Ortiz thanked Nia for returning the apron, then smiled at the sign. “You returned more than what you found,” she said.

questions.stimulusTitle: Measuring a Tree Without Climbing It
questions.stimulusText:
Foresters often need to estimate a tree’s height without climbing it. One simple method uses shadows and similar triangles. On a sunny day, a person places a straight measuring stick upright on level ground near the tree. The stick and tree cast shadows at the same time. Because sunlight reaches both objects at the same angle, the two objects and their shadows form triangles with matching angles.
The forester measures the stick, its shadow, and the tree’s shadow. Suppose a one-meter stick casts a two-meter shadow while a tree casts a thirty-meter shadow. The tree is fifteen times taller than the stick because its shadow is fifteen times longer. Its estimated height is therefore fifteen meters.
Accuracy depends on careful conditions. The stick must stand vertically, and both shadows should fall across ground with a similar slope. Blurred shadow tips can make endpoints difficult to judge. Wind may also move branches, changing the apparent end of the tree’s shadow. Taking several measurements and averaging the results can reduce the effect of small errors.
This method does not provide a perfect measurement, but it allows foresters to gather useful information quickly with ordinary tools.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What change did Varga make after testers struggled with a narrow handle?

choices.A: She removed the handle.
choices.B: She added measurement labels.
choices.C: She made it wider and textured.
choices.D: She replaced the early model with a jar.

questions.correctAnswer: She made it wider and textured.
questions.explanation: Varga widened the narrow handle and added texture after observing testers.
questions.stimulusText:
As a young craft worker, Elena Varga repaired household tools in a busy neighborhood shop. She noticed that many customers struggled with ordinary objects for reasons manufacturers had overlooked. A jar opener might require a strong grip. A measuring cup might have markings visible from only one side. Instead of blaming users, Varga began asking how the objects could change.
Years later, as a product designer, she invited people of different ages and abilities to test early models. Their comments often altered her plans. When testers had difficulty turning a narrow handle, she made it wider and added a textured surface. When left-handed users covered measurement labels while pouring, she printed labels on both sides.
Some colleagues worried that these changes would make products complicated. Varga argued that thoughtful features could simplify an object for nearly everyone. A broad handle helped a person with limited grip strength, but it also helped a cook whose hands were wet. Labels on both sides assisted left-handed users and anyone viewing the cup from an unusual angle.
Varga’s greatest contribution was not a single invention. It was her habit of treating difficulty as information. By observing where people hesitated, she discovered opportunities to design objects that welcomed more users.
